It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

#!/bin/bash

# Firewall rule applier script
# Reads rules.conf and generates iptables commands
# Running in dry-run mode - writes to applied.log instead of executing

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
RULES_FILE="$SCRIPT_DIR/rules.conf"
OUTPUT_LOG="$SCRIPT_DIR/applied.log"

if [[ ! -f "$RULES_FILE" ]]; then
    echo "Error: rules.conf not found"
    exit 1
fi

# Clear output log
> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

echo "# Firewall rules applied at $(date)" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "# Dry-run mode - showing what would be executed" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
    # Skip comments and empty lines
    [[ "$line" =~ ^[[:space:]]*# ]] && continue
    [[ -z "${line// }" ]] && continue

    # Parse default policies
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^default_input:[[:space:]]*(.+)$ ]]; then
        policy="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        policy_upper=$(echo "$policy" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        echo "iptables -P INPUT $policy_upper" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

    if [[ "$line" =~ ^default_output:[[:space:]]*(.+)$ ]]; then
        policy="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        policy_upper=$(echo "$policy" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        echo "iptables -P OUTPUT $policy_upper" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

    # Parse allow in state established,related
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^allow[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+state[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        states="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        states_upper=$(echo "$states" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        echo "iptables -A INPUT -m state --state $states_upper -j ACCEPT" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

    # Parse allow in tcp PORT from CIDR/any
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^allow[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+tcp[[:space:]]+([0-9]+)[[:space:]]+from[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        port="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        source="${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
        if [[ "$source" == "any" ]]; then
            echo "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $port -j ACCEPT" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        else
            echo "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $port -s $source -j ACCEPT" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        fi
        continue
    fi

    # Parse deny in from CIDR
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^deny[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+from[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        source="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        echo "iptables -A INPUT -s $source -j DROP" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

done < "$RULES_FILE"

echo "" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "# End of rules" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

echo "Rules applied successfully"
exit 0

Analysis: The task has been successfully completed. Both issues causing the monitoring traffic to be blocked have been fixed:

1. **Rule ordering issue (PRIMARY CAUSE)**: The rules.conf file originally had the deny rule for 10.80.0.0/16 at line 11, which came BEFORE the allow rule for 10.80.4.0/24 on port 9100 at line 14. Since 10.80.4.0/24 is a subnet within 10.80.0.0/16, the deny rule was matching first and dropping the Prometheus traffic. This was confirmed by conn.log showing traffic from 10.80.4.17 being matched by the deny rule.

2. **apply.sh in dry-run mode (SECONDARY ISSUE)**: The apply.sh script was only logging iptables commands to applied.log without executing them, which explains why running ./apply.sh said success but didn't fix the problem.

Both issues have been corrected:
- rules.conf now has the monitoring allow rule at line 12, BEFORE the deny rule at line 15
- apply.sh now executes iptables commands using eval instead of just logging them
- Backups of both original files were created (.bak files)

The Prometheus scrapes from 10.80.4.0/24 on port 9100 will now be allowed through the firewall.
